Temperature dependence of the electronic structure of semiconductors and insulators

August 24, 2026
Abstract

The renormalization of electronic eigenenergies due to electron-phonon coupling (temperature dependence and zero-point motion effect) is sizeable in many materials with light atoms. This effect, often neglected in ab-initio calculations, can be computed using the perturbation-based Allen-Heine-Cardona theory in the adiabatic or non-adiabatic harmonic approximation. After a short description of the numerous recent progresses in this field, and a brief overview of the theory, we focus on the issue of phonon wavevector sampling convergence, until now poorly understood. Indeed, the renormalization is obtained numerically through a (usually slowly converging) 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sampling inside the Brillouin Zone. For 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points close to Γ\Gamma, we show that a divergence due to non-zero Born effective charge appears in the electron-phonon matrix elements, leading to a divergence of the integral over the (phonon) Brillouin zone for band extrema. Although it should vanish for non-polar materials, unphysical residual Born effective charges are usually present in ab-initio calculations. Here, we propose a solution that improves the coupled (electronic) 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point convergence dramatically. For polar materials, the problem is more severe: the divergence of the integral does not disappear in the adiabatic harmonic approximation, but only in the non-adiabatic harmonic approximation. In all cases, we study in detail the convergence behavior of the renormalization as the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sampling goes to infinity and the imaginary broadening broadening parameter goes to zero. This allows extrapolation, thus enabling a systematic way to converge the renormalization for both polar and non-polar materials. Finally, the adiabatic and non-adiabatic theory, with corrections for the divergence problem, are applied to the study of five semiconductors and insulators: α\alpha-AlN, β\beta-AlN, BN, diamond and silicon. For these five materials, we present the zero-point renormalization, temperature dependence, phonon-induced lifetime broadening and the renormalized electronic bandstructure.

I Introduction

The theoretical understanding of the effects of the electron-phonon coupling on the electronic structure and the capability to compute them have a long and chaotic history that started in the early fifties. Over the years, these effects have been computed using three types of methods, with different advantages and drawbacks: (1) as a time average of the bandgap using first-principles molecular dynamics (MD) simulations; (2) through the frozen-phonon (FP) method, which weights the eigenenergy change along the phonon modes with a Bose-Einstein distribution; (3) thanks to the diagrammatic method of many-body perturbation theory. For a historical review, the reader can consult Ref. 1, in which these three types of methods are compared to each other, at the harmonic level.

In the present contribution, we rely on the Allen-Heine-Cardona (AHC) theory [2, 3, 4] to compute the zero-point motion renormalization as well as the temperature dependence of electronic eigenenergies. The AHC theory originates from the diagrammatic method of many-body perturbation theory. It has been applied in several recent milestone contributions in the field, including the computation of temperature-dependence of the optical properties [5], the computation of the surprisingly large zero-point renormalization (ZPR) of the diamond bandgap [6, 7], the demonstration of large non-rigid ion corrections for molecules [8], the inclusion of dynamical effects beyond the adiabatic approximation [9, 10, 11], the study of the anharmonic electron-phonon contribution to the indirect bandgap of diamond [12], and the inclusion of electronic many-body effects (in the GW approximation) in diamond [13], noticing a large increase of the renormalization with respect to density-functional theory (DFT). Also, we think that the confusion in the theoretical understanding of the relationship between MD, FP, and AHC as well as the inaccuracies in first-principles software implementations of AHC have been largely eliminated in two recent publications [7, 1].

One of the major issues when performing AHC calculations is the slow convergence with respect to phonon wavevector sampling of the Brillouin Zone (BZ) [7], refereed to as 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sampling from now on. To accelerate this convergence, a small imaginary component i​δi\delta (which can be inferred as a finite lifetime for the unoccupied electronic states due to thermal effects) is often used. However, this imaginary parameter is ad hoc rather than ab-initio. Also, the convergence problem is even more severe with the MD and FP methods, as supercells have to be used to sample the phonons wavevectors, thus dramatically increasing the computational time and memory required. Actually, numerical convergence for the MD and FP methods cannot really be reached in three-dimensional solids, in contrast with finite systems [7, 13, 14].

In this paper, we highlight that when trying to converge the ZPR with respect to 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sampling for vanishing i​δi\delta in the AHC simulations, the ZPR diverges. For non-polar materials, such unphysical divergence is attributed to a residual Born effective charge, which stems from the finite 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point sampling. We propose a solution to this problem and devise a systematic way to converge the ZPR for vanishing i​δi\delta. For polar materials, the problem is more profound. Indeed, the divergence in the adiabatic AHC approach is not simply numerical, but indicates a breakdown of the AHC approach. A similar problem should also be present in the MD and FT methods. On the other hand, the non-adiabatic AHC theory naturally leads to non-diverging quantities.

This paper is organized as follow. First, a short reminder of the AHC theory is presented in section II. In Sec. III, the bottleneck of the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point convergence is discussed, the divergence problem of the ZPR at large 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point density is explored and a solution is proposed. We also device in sections IV and V a systematic and parameter free way to extrapolate the ZPR (without i​δi\delta). Finally in section VI, we present the temperature dependences, the zero-point motion renormalizations, as well as the phonon-induced lifetimes for five semiconductors: α\alpha-AlN, β\beta-AlN, BN, diamond and silicon.

II Review of the Allen-Heine-Cardona formalism

II.1 The AHC theory within the adiabatic harmonic approximation

The temperature-dependent renormalization of the electronic eigenenergy εn​𝐤\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}} for band nn and wavevector 𝐤\mathbf{k} can be written in the adiabatic harmonic approximation as a sum over the BZ of the phonon contributions for each wavevector 𝐪\mathbf{q} [1]

Δ​εn​𝐤​(T)=1Nq​∑𝐪∑m3​N∂εn​𝐤∂nm​𝐪​(nm​𝐪​(T)+12),\Delta\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}(T)=\frac{1}{N_{q}}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\sum_{m}^{3N}\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}\Big(n_{m\mathbf{q}}(T)+\frac{1}{2}\Big), (1)

with

∂εn​𝐤∂nm​𝐪=12​ωm​𝐪​∑κ​ακ′​γ∑l​l′∂2εn​𝐤∂Rl​κ​α​∂Rl′​κ′​γe−i𝐪⋅(𝐑l−𝐑l′)Um,κ′​γ∗(𝐪)Um,κ​α(𝐪),\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}=\frac{1}{2\omega_{m\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}\sum_{ll^{\prime}}\frac{\partial^{2}\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}}{\partial R_{l\kappa\alpha}\partial R_{l^{\prime}\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}}\\ e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{R}_{l}-\mathbf{R}_{l^{\prime}})}U_{m,\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}^{*}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q}), (2)

where mm is the phonon branch, TT is the temperature, NqN_{q} is the number of wavevectors used to sample the BZ, ωm​𝐪\omega_{m\mathbf{q}} is the phonon frequency, nm​𝐪​(T)=1eωm​𝐪kB​T−1n_{m\mathbf{q}}(T)=\frac{1}{e^{\frac{\omega_{m\mathbf{q}}}{k_{B}T}}-1} is the Bose-Einstein distribution, Um,κ​α​(𝐪)U_{m,\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q}) is the eigendisplacement vector of atom κ\kappa in direction α\alpha associated to the phonon mode, and ∂/∂Rl​κ​α\partial/\partial R_{l\kappa\alpha} is the derivative of a quantity with respect to the displacement of atom κ\kappa of the unit cell ll in the direction α\alpha.

The quantity Δ​εn​𝐤​(T)≜εn​𝐤​(T)−εn​𝐤​[0]\Delta\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}(T)\triangleq\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}(T)-\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}[0] is the difference between the temperature-dependent eigenenergy and the eigenenergy at ground-state atomic positions. We distinguish the temperature-dependent εn​𝐤\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}} from the atomic-position-dependent εn​𝐤\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}} by using ()() in the former and [][] in the latter. The difference between εn​𝐤​(T=0)\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}(T=0) and εn​𝐤​[0]\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}[0] is called the zero-point motion renormalization (ZPR).

In a mean field approximation like the Density Functional Theory (DFT), the eigenenergies are the expectation values of the Hamiltonian H^𝐤,𝐤\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k,k}} of the system

εn​𝐤=⟨un​𝐤(0)|​H^𝐤,𝐤​|un​𝐤(0)⟩,\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}=\Bra{u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}}\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k,k}}\Ket{u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}}, (3)

with un​𝐤(0)u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)} the periodic part of the electronic wavefunctions. Using perturbation theory to obtain the second-order derivative with respect to atomic displacements of such eigenenergies, Eq. (2) can be rewritten as

where (c.c.)(c.c.) stands for the complex conjugate of the previous terms within parenthesis (), and where we use the following notation for the derivative with respect to atomic positions of an arbitrary quantity XX

∂X∂Rκ​α​(𝐪)=1NB​v​K​∑lei​𝐪⋅𝐑l​∂X∂Rl​κ​α,\frac{\partial X}{\partial R_{\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q})}=\frac{1}{N_{BvK}}\sum_{l}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{R}_{l}}\frac{\partial X}{\partial R_{l\kappa\alpha}}, (5)

The first term within {}\{\} in Eq. (4) is called the Debye-Waller (DW) term

𝒟κ​ακ′​γ​(𝐪)≜⟨un​𝐤(0)|∂2H^𝐤,𝐤∂Rκ​α​(−𝐪)​∂Rκ′​γ​(𝐪)|un​𝐤(0)⟩,\mathcal{D}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{q})\triangleq\Big\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}\Big|\frac{\partial^{2}\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k,k}}}{\partial R_{\kappa\alpha}(-\mathbf{q})\partial R_{\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}(\mathbf{q})}\Big|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}\Big\rangle, (6)

ℱκ​ακ′​γ(𝐪)≜12[((⟨∂un​𝐤∂Rκ​α​(𝐪)|∂H^𝐤,𝐤∂Rκ′​γ​(𝐪)|un​𝐤(0)⟩+(κα)↔(κ′γ))+(c.c.))].\begin{split}\mathcal{F}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{q})\triangleq\frac{1}{2}\bigg[\bigg(\Big(\Big\langle\frac{\partial u_{n\mathbf{k}}}{\partial R_{\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q})}\Big|\frac{\partial\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k,k}}}{\partial R_{\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}(\mathbf{q})}\Big|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}\Big\rangle\\ +(\kappa\alpha)\leftrightarrow(\kappa^{\prime}\gamma)\Big)+(c.c.)\bigg)\bigg].\end{split} (7)

The change of eigenenergy due to a specific phonon mode (e.g. Eq. (4)) thus becomes

∂εn​𝐤∂nm​𝐪≜∂εn​𝐤FAN∂nm​𝐪+∂εn​𝐤DW∂nm​𝐪,\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}\triangleq\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{FAN}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}+\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{DW}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}, (8)

∂εn​𝐤FAN∂nm​𝐪≜12​ωm​𝐪​∑κ​ακ′​γℱκ​ακ′​γ​(𝐪)​Um,κ′​γ∗​(𝐪)​Um,κ​α​(𝐪),\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{FAN}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}\triangleq\frac{1}{2\omega_{m\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}\mathcal{F}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}^{*}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q}), (9)

(10)

At this point, no approximations beyond the adiabatic and harmonic ones were made. However, the calculation of the Debye-Waller term (Eq. (6)) requires the second-order derivative of the Hamiltonian, which is a computational bottleneck within the density functional perturbation theory (DFPT) framework. To overcome this issue, we make the rigid-ion approximation (RIA) as is usual within the AHC theory  [2, 3, 4]. We begin by splitting the DW term into two parts. The first part contains all contributions that can be computed using first-order derivatives of the Hamiltonians, while the second part contains the remaining contributions

∂εn​𝐤DW∂nm​𝐪=∂εn​𝐤DWRIA∂nm​𝐪+∂εn​𝐤DWNRIA∂nm​𝐪,\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{DW}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}=\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{DW}_{\text{RIA}}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}+\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{DW}_{\text{NRIA}}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}, (11)

with

∂εn​𝐤DWRIA∂nm​𝐪=−14​ωm​𝐪​∑κ​ακ′​γℱκ​ακ′​γ​(𝚪)(Um,κ​γ∗​(𝐪)​Um,κ​α​(𝐪)+Um,κ′​γ∗​(𝐪)​Um,κ′​α​(𝐪)),\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{DW}_{\text{RIA}}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}=\frac{-1}{4\omega_{m\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}\mathcal{F}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma})\\ \Big(U_{m,\kappa\gamma}^{*}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q})+U_{m,\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}^{*}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa^{\prime}\alpha}(\mathbf{q})\Big), (12)

∂εn​𝐤DWNRIA∂nm​𝐪=12​ωm​𝐪∑κ​ακ′​γ[𝒟κ​ακ′​γ(𝐪)Um,κ′​γ∗(𝐪)Um,κ​α(𝐪)−12𝒟κ​ακ′​γ(𝚪)(Um,κ​γ∗(𝐪)Um,κ​α(𝐪)+Um,κ′​γ∗(𝐪)Um,κ′​α(𝐪))].\frac{\partial\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{\text{DW}_{\text{NRIA}}}}{\partial n_{m\mathbf{q}}}=\\ \frac{1}{2\omega_{m\mathbf{q}}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}\bigg[\mathcal{D}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}^{*}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q})-\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{D}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\kappa\alpha\\ \kappa^{\prime}\gamma\end{subarray}}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma})\\ \Big(U_{m,\kappa\gamma}^{*}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q})+U_{m,\kappa^{\prime}\gamma}^{*}(\mathbf{q})U_{m,\kappa^{\prime}\alpha}(\mathbf{q})\Big)\bigg]. (13)

For example, in the case of diamond, several authors have used an i​δi\delta of 100 meV to account for the finite lifetimes of the electronic states [17, 6, 13, 7]. However, the theory must also be valid (apart from controlled numerical instabilities) for vanishing i​δi\delta. This point will be further discussed in section III.

II.2 Beyond the Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory

Phonons alter the one-electron energy bands εn​𝐤\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}} in two ways: there is a shift Δ​εn​𝐤\Delta\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}} and a lifetime broadening 1/τn​𝐤1/\tau_{n\mathbf{k}}. As seen in the previous sub-section, the adiabatic approximation leads to a real renormalization of the eigenstates. The study of the lifetime broadening requires an extension of the adiabatic theory.

In 1978, Allen generalized his earlier work [2] derived within the standard Rayleigh-Schrödinger perturbation theory to include finite phonon frequencies using many-body perturbation techniques [18]. These techniques describe excitations in terms of spectral functions [10], where quasiparticules cannot always be unambiguously identified, with the associated well defined eigenenergies. In this work, following Allen [18], rather than obtaining the full spectral function to describe the electronic excitation, we suppose that their description in terms of quasiparticles is still valid and evaluate the associated eigenenergies by correcting the DFT eigenvalues to first-order in perturbation theory, taking the self-energy evaluated at ω=εn​𝐤(0)\omega=\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)} as the perturbation. Complex eigenenergies are obtained within this generalization, that we refer to as the “non-adiabatic” extension of the AHC theory εn​𝐤​(T,ω)\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}(T,\omega) [18, 19].

We therefore obtain the following equation, based on electron-phonon matrix elements already calculated for the adiabatic renormalization

III Phonon wavevector sampling and the divergence problem

III.1 Potential breakdown of perturbation theory

Quantum mechanical perturbation theory can breakdown when vanishing denominators appear in the perturbation series. This can happen in the present case, as the short-hand form of Eq. (15) is

Δ​εn​𝐤(adiabatic,RIA)​(T)∝∑𝐪|G​K​K​(𝐪)|2ε𝐤(0)−ε𝐤+𝐪(0).\Delta\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(\text{adiabatic,RIA})}(T)\propto\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\frac{|GKK(\mathbf{q})|^{2}}{\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}-\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k+q}}^{(0)}}. (19)

Actually, there are two types of potential divergences in Eq. (19): (i) when ε𝐤(0)=ε𝐤+𝐪(0)\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}=\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k+q}}^{(0)} and (ii) when the electron-phonon matrix elements G​K​K​(𝐪)GKK(\mathbf{q}) diverge, which happens when the sum of Born effective charges does not vanish, as we shall see (G​K​K​(𝐪)GKK(\mathbf{q}) is then proportional to 1𝐪\frac{1}{\mathbf{q}}).

In practical calculations, the 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q=0} contribution from the same band (the denominator being thus zero) is not included in the summation. Also, in case of degeneracies, the terms with zero denominators are ignored. However, the integral of these divergences still needs to be obtained through the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point summation. For this reason, the numerical convergence of the adiabatic ZPR of diamond with respect to 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point density is slow and requires large 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grids [7]. This problem is often assessed in practice by adding an ad-hoc i​δi\delta to the denominator of Eq. (19).

The dipoles present in polar materials induce a Born effective charge, which describes the coupling between the electric field generated by the dipoles and the ionic motion. Such Born effective charges lead to a 1𝐪\frac{1}{\mathbf{q}} behavior of the electron-phonon matrix elements (GKK). Divergences of type (ii) are therefore present in these materials. However, in non-polar materials, there are theoretically no such effective charges and there should therefore be no divergence of type (ii). Since divergences of type (i) have a finite integral when no divergence of type (ii) are present, the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sum should convergence to a finite value for non-polar materials.

In practice, however, we observed a non-physical divergence of the ZPR for large 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points densities. This effect can be clearly seen in Figure 1, where the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point density dependence of the adiabatic Γ25v\Gamma_{25}^{v} ZPR of diamond (calculated using Eq. (15)) for vanishing i​δi\delta exhibits a divergent behavior when δ\delta is 1 meV or 0.01 meV, hardly seen for δ\delta equal to 50 meV or 100 meV.

Actually, this divergence is attributed to a residual electric field connected to the breaking of the Born effective charge neutrality sum rule in non-polar periodic solids. This leads to the presence of divergences of type (ii), which combined to these of type (i), give an infinite integral around 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q=0}, thus making the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sum diverge.

This residual electric field is due to the finite 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point grid used within DFT. Indeed, the first-order density is obtained thanks to a discretized integral on the BZ (see Eq. (B9) of Ref. 20). This first-order density in turn determines the electric field and the Born effective charges (see Eq. (42) of Ref. 21). Such residual electric field that breaks the charge neutrality is found to converge to zero exponentially but is nonetheless substantial at 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point grid usually sufficient to converge other relevant quantities. An example of this slow convergence is given in Table 1 for the case of diamond (a non-polar material).

III.2 Restoration of the charge neutrality

In this section, we present a scheme to numerically remove this spurious electric field, and thus considerably speed up the ZPR convergence with respect to the electronic wavevector sampling. To this end, let us study the impact of a small Born effective charge on the matrix elements of ∂H^𝐤,𝐤∂Rκ​α​(𝐪)\frac{\partial\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k,k}}}{\partial R_{\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q})} present in Eq. (15). We introduce the following short-hand notation for derivatives, which matches the one used in Ref. 20

∂H^𝐤,𝐤∂Rκ​α​(𝐪)≜H𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1).\frac{\partial\hat{H}_{\mathbf{k,k}}}{\partial R_{\kappa\alpha}(\mathbf{q})}\triangleq H_{\mathbf{k+q,k}}^{(1)}. (20)

As mentioned in Ref. 20, within the pseudopotential framework, H𝐪(1)H_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)} can be decomposed into a first-order change of the non-local, local, Hartree and exchange-correlation potentials:

H𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)=vs​e​p,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)+v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1)+v¯H,𝐪(1)+v¯x​c,𝐪(1),H_{\mathbf{k+q,k}}^{(1)}=v_{sep,\mathbf{k+q,k}}^{(1)}+\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}+\bar{v}_{H,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}+\bar{v}_{xc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}, (21)

where the bar symbol above a quantity X¯\bar{X} means that it is the periodic part of XX

X¯𝐪(1)(𝐫)=e−i𝐪⋅𝐫X𝐪(1)(𝐫),\bar{X}_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r})=e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}X_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r}), (22)

and where both v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1)\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)} and v¯H,𝐪(1)\bar{v}_{H,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)} diverge as 1|𝐪|\frac{1}{\mathbf{|q|}} with opposite signs.

To make this more explicit, we express v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1)\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)} as

v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1)(𝐆)=−iΩ0(𝐆+𝐪)αe−i(𝐆+𝐪)⋅𝝉κvκl​o​c(𝐆+𝐪),\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G})=\frac{-i}{\Omega_{0}}(\mathbf{G+q})_{\alpha}e^{-i(\mathbf{G+q})\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\kappa}}v_{\kappa}^{loc}(\mathbf{G+q}), (23)

where Ω0\Omega_{0} is the volume of the unperturbed unit cell, 𝝉κ\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\kappa} the vector position of the atom κ\kappa in the unit cell and with

vκl​o​c​(𝐪→0)=−4​π​Zκq2+Cκ+𝒪⁡(q2).v_{\kappa}^{loc}(\mathbf{q}\rightarrow 0)=-\frac{4\pi Z_{\kappa}}{q^{2}}+C_{\kappa}+\mathcal{O}(q^{2}). (24)

To also explicit the same behavior in v¯H,𝐪(1)\bar{v}_{H,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}, we express it as

v¯H,𝐪(1)​(𝐆)=4​π​n¯𝐪(1)|𝐆+𝐪|2,\bar{v}_{H,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G})=4\pi\frac{\bar{n}_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}}{|\mathbf{G+q}|^{2}}, (25)

where n¯𝐪(1)∝|𝐪|\bar{n}_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}\propto\mathbf{|q|} when 𝐪→𝟎\mathbf{q}\rightarrow\mathbf{0}.

The v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1)​(𝐆)\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G}) of Eq. (23) has an explicit algebraic form for 𝐪→0\mathbf{q}\rightarrow 0, where ZκZ_{\kappa} is the number of valence electrons of the atom κ\kappa described in the pseudopotential. Therefore, a residual electric charge can only affect the first-order density n¯𝐪(1)\bar{n}_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)} in Eq. (25). The derivation of the impact of a residual Born effective charge on the first-order density is presented in Appendix A of this paper and can be seen in Eq. (139) in the 𝐆=𝟎\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{0} limit.

Using this knowledge, we can renormalize the Hartree term as follow (see Eq. (143))

v¯H,𝐪r​e​n​(1)​(𝟎)=v¯H,𝐪(1)​(𝟎)​∑γqγ​(Zκ​δα​γ−(Zκ​α,γ∗−Z¯α​γ)1q2​∑δ,ξqδ​ϵδ​ξ​qξ)∑γqγ​(Zκ​δα​γ−Zκ​α,γ∗1q2​∑δ,ξqδ​ϵδ​ξ​qξ),\bar{v}_{H,\mathbf{q}}^{ren(1)}(\mathbf{0})=\\ \bar{v}_{H,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{0})\frac{\sum_{\gamma}q_{\gamma}\Big(Z_{\kappa}\delta_{\alpha\gamma}-\frac{(Z_{\kappa\alpha,\gamma}^{*}-\bar{Z}_{\alpha\gamma})}{\frac{1}{q^{2}}\sum_{\delta,\xi}q_{\delta}\epsilon_{\delta\xi}q_{\xi}}\Big)}{\sum_{\gamma}q_{\gamma}\Big(Z_{\kappa}\delta_{\alpha\gamma}-\frac{Z_{\kappa\alpha,\gamma}^{*}}{\frac{1}{q^{2}}\sum_{\delta,\xi}q_{\delta}\epsilon_{\delta\xi}q_{\xi}}\Big)}, (26)

where Zκ,α​β∗Z_{\kappa,\alpha\beta}^{*} is the Born effective charge, ϵγ​ξ\epsilon_{\gamma\xi} is the macroscopic static dielectric tensor for the electronic system (where the ions are considered fixed) and Z¯α​β\bar{Z}_{\alpha\beta} is the averaged Born effective charge

Z¯α​β=1Na​t​∑κZκ,α​β∗,\bar{Z}_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{1}{N_{at}}\sum_{\kappa}Z_{\kappa,\alpha\beta}^{*}, (27)

where Na​tN_{at} is the number of atoms in the primitive cell. If the charge neutrality sum rule was fulfilled, the averaged Born effective charge should be exactly zero.

With this renormalization, the v¯H,𝐪r​e​n​(1)\bar{v}_{H,\mathbf{q}}^{ren(1)} term correctly cancels the v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1)\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)} when 𝐪→0\mathbf{q}\rightarrow 0. Figure 2 clearly shows the faster convergence rate of the ZPR with respect to the density of the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point grid obtained with this renormalization for the specific case of the first band of diamond at 𝐤=𝐋\mathbf{k}=\mathbf{L}. To highlight the divergent behavior of the ZPR with respect to 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid density without the associated high computational cost for 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point integration, only 6 symmetry equivalent 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points are used in the sum. The 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points are chosen close enough to zero to show the divergence: 𝐪=1100​𝐗\mathbf{q}=\frac{1}{100}\mathbf{X}.

IV Behavior of the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point convergence

After enforcing the charge neutrality by application of Eq. (26), the theoretical rate of convergence of the ZPR can be analyzed when the number of 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points along a side of the Brillouin Zone NqN_{q} increases (the total number of q-points in the Brillouin Zone is Nq3N_{q}^{3}). After isolating the divergent behavior, we will analyze analytically, and numerically on simple models, the rate of convergence of the ZPR.

We will observe that the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point convergence can be either constant, linear (1/Nq1/N_{q}) or divergent (NqN_{q}) depending on the state that is renormalized, the use of the adiabatic (Eq. (15)) or non-adiabatic (Eq. (16)) equation as well as the polar or non-polar nature of the material. The table (2) gives a summary of those behavior.

IV.1 Rapid convergence with NqN_{q}

The corrected (using Eq. (26)) electron-phonon matrix elements of non-polar materials have no strong 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point dependence. Also, if the state of interest (n​𝐤n\mathbf{k}) is a valence band maximum (VBM) or a conduction band minimum (CBM), the band dispersion is quadratic in reciprocal space around 𝐤\mathbf{k}, and therefore εn​𝐤−εn′​𝐤+𝐪\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{n^{\prime}\mathbf{k+q}} behaves as q2q^{2}.

IV.1.1 Non-polar materials in the non-adiabatic approximation at VBM/CBM

For a non-polar material within the non-adiabatic approximation (Eq. (16)), we can model the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point behavior of the ZPR of the VBM with

limδ→0∭0qcd3​q​1εn​𝐤−εn′​𝐤+𝐪+ω𝐪+i​δ,\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\iiint_{0}^{q_{c}}d^{3}q\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{n^{\prime}\mathbf{k+q}}+\omega_{\mathbf{q}}+i\delta}, (28)

where qq is integrated in a sphere of radius qcq_{c}. The same derivation applies for the CBM with −ω𝐪-\omega_{\mathbf{q}}, the energy difference εn​𝐤−εn​𝐤+𝐪\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k+q}} being negative. The phonon frequency shifts the poles of the function, so that the integrand is analytic over the domain of integration. The parabolic behavior of the extrema leads to

=limδ→0∭0qcd3​q​1q2+ω+i​δ\displaystyle=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\iiint_{0}^{q_{c}}d^{3}q\frac{1}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta} (29)
=limδ→0∫0qcd​q​∫−ππd​ϕ​∫0πd​θ​q2​sin⁡θq2+ω+i​δ\displaystyle=\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\int_{0}^{q_{c}}dq\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\phi\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta\frac{q^{2}\sin\theta}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta} (30)
=∫0qcd​q​4​π​q2q2+ω\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{q_{c}}dq4\pi\frac{q^{2}}{q^{2}+\omega} (31)
=4​π​ω​(qcω−tan−1⁡(qcω)).\displaystyle=4\pi\sqrt{\omega}\Big(\frac{q_{c}}{\sqrt{\omega}}-\tan^{-1}\big(\frac{q_{c}}{\sqrt{\omega}}\big)\Big). (32)

A Taylor expansion around qc=0q_{c}=0 reveals that

4​π​ω​(qcω−tan−1⁡(qcω))=4​π​ω3​(qcω)3+𝒪⁡(qc5),4\pi\sqrt{\omega}\Big(\frac{q_{c}}{\sqrt{\omega}}-\tan^{-1}\big(\frac{q_{c}}{\sqrt{\omega}}\big)\Big)\\ =\frac{4\pi\sqrt{\omega}}{3}\Big(\frac{q_{c}}{\sqrt{\omega}}\Big)^{3}+\mathcal{O}(q_{c}^{5}), (33)

which means that the contribution from the integration around q=0q=0 is simply proportional to the volume of integration, as expected given the non-divergent nature of the integrand.

Thus, neglecting the q=0q=0 contribution in the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sum of the non-adiabatic ZPR for a band extrema of a non-polar material causes an error proportional to 1Nq3\frac{1}{N_{q}^{3}} whereas discretization of the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point integration over the Brillouin Zone with the rectangle method causes an error proportional to 1Nq2\frac{1}{N_{q}^{2}}. Therefore, the error caused by the neglected q=0q=0 contribution is not visible in the global convergence behavior for this ZPR. This behavior will be referred to as “flat” convergence with respect to 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid density from now on.

Additionally, we can numerically integrate Eq. (28) on a three dimensional grid of 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points using

VNq3​∑q1q2+ω+i​δ,\frac{V}{N_{q}^{3}}\sum_{q}\frac{1}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta}, (34)

where VV is the volume of integration and where the element of volume is inversely proportional to the number of 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points Nq3N_{q}^{3} needed to discretized the grid. An example of the convergence of Eq. (34) with 1Nq\frac{1}{N_{q}} is shown on the top of Figure 3 for qc=0.5q_{c}=0.5 and ω=0.01\omega=0.01.

This function converges very quickly with increasing 𝐪\mathbf{q}-sampling as can be seen e.g. on the center of Figure 6a for the VBM of diamond using the non-adiabatic equation.

IV.1.2 Non-polar materials in the adiabatic or non-adiabatic approximation for a non-extremal band

If the state that we would like to renormalize is not a VBM nor a CBM, the denominator of the adiabatic (Eq. (15)) or non-adiabatic (Eq. (16)) equations will be small when the state that we consider (εn​𝐤\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}) has almost the same energy as another state (εn′​𝐤+𝐪\varepsilon_{n^{\prime}\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}), minus a phonon frequency (ωm​𝐪\omega_{m\mathbf{q}}) in the non-adiabatic framework. As a result, the integrand in Eq. (28) is not analytic anymore in these cases and a non-zero imaginary i​δi\delta is required to avoid numerical instabilities.

To get a deeper understanding of the behavior of non-extremal points, we will model the energy difference (εn​𝐤−εn′​𝐤+𝐪\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{n^{\prime}\mathbf{k+q}}) by a shifted parabola with its minimum at 𝐪0\mathbf{q}_{0}

ε𝐤−ε𝐤+𝐪=(𝐪−𝐪0)2−q02.\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}-\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}=(\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{q}_{0})^{2}-q_{0}^{2}. (35)

The ZPR has poles on a sphere of radius q0q_{0} centered on 𝐪=𝐪𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{q_{0}} (chosen to be on the z-axis) and passing through the origin. The integral on the spherical shell between radii of values q0−Δq_{0}-\Delta and q0+Δq_{0}+\Delta gives a contribution that is linear with Δ\Delta (see Appendix B.1), as would any regular function when integrated over a spherical shell. This indicates that the integration of these poles will not contribute an error of higher order than the reminder of the numerical integration. Neglecting the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 contribution in the numerical integration leads to an error proportional to 1Nq3\frac{1}{N_{q}^{3}} in the non-polar case (see Appendix B.2). This leads to a 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid convergence that is flat for the non-polar case in the adiabatic framework.

In the non-adiabatic case, the ω\omega to be added to the right-hand side of Eq. (35) only slightly reduces the radius of the sphere at 𝐪0\mathbf{q}_{0} (which thus does not touch the origin anymore) and the conclusion for the adiabatic case remains valid for the numerical integration over this sphere. The integrand at 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0} becomes analytical in this case, so that the convergence behavior remains effectively flat. Therefore, in practice, the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point integration required to evaluate the ZPR can be considered converged when the ZPR does not change significantly with denser grids. An example of this type of convergence is given at the top of Figure 5a for diamond in the adiabatic framework at a non-extremal energy.

In other cases, the discretized integral does not converge as quickly as the rectangle method for an analytical integrand. It sometimes converges linearly (∝1Nq\propto\frac{1}{N_{q}}) (see subsection IV.2) or even diverges (∝Nq\propto N_{q}) (see subsection IV.3).

IV.2 Convergence proportional to the inverse of NqN_{q}

IV.2.1 Non-polar materials in the adiabatic approximation at the VBM/CBM

Non-polar materials with a parabolic energy dispersion (VBM or CBM) have a 𝐪\mathbf{q}-dependence for the adiabatic ZPR that behaves as

∭0qcd3​q​1q2+i​δ=4​π​qc∝1Nq,\iiint_{0}^{q_{c}}d^{3}q\frac{1}{q^{2}+i\delta}=4\pi q_{c}\propto\frac{1}{N_{q}}, (36)

when i​δ=0i\delta=0. Therefore, neglecting the q=0q=0 contribution in the numerical integration yields an error proportional to 1Nq\frac{1}{N_{q}} that dominates the 1Nq2\frac{1}{N_{q}^{2}} error of the rectangle method. We will call this type of convergence “linear” here.

The rate of convergence with 𝐪\mathbf{q}-densification can be numerically tested by summing this function on a three dimensional grid of 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points

1Nq3​∑q≠01q2+i​δ,\frac{1}{N_{q}^{3}}\sum_{q\neq 0}\frac{1}{q^{2}+i\delta}, (37)

where the q=0q=0 term has been omitted in the sum for numerical reasons (as the expression must stand for vanishing δ\delta). The numerical integral of Eq. (37) is shown on Figure 4 and converges towards 2​π2\pi for q0=0.5q_{0}=0.5, as expected.

IV.2.2 Polar materials in the adiabatic (non-extremal point) and non-adiabatic approximation

In the case of polar materials, the GKK behaves as 1/q21/q^{2} for small qq, but this time, the divergence is physical and comes from the physical finite Born effective charges. In this case, at the VBM or CBM, the non-adiabatic Eq. (16) shifts the pole inside the bandgap. Therefore, the parabolic eigenenergy dispersion is not problematic anymore. This can be represented by

ℜ∭0qcd3q1q2​(ω+i​δ).\Re\iiint_{0}^{q_{c}}d^{3}q\frac{1}{q^{2}(\omega+i\delta)}. (38)

This case behaves as Eq. (37) and we have the same linear behavior because the diverging 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q=0} term is removed from the numerical sum.

In the case of points that are not at a VBM or a CBM, the integration of the ZPR in the adiabatic and non-adiabatic approximations exhibits a behavior that is linear with 1/Nq1/N_{q}. This is explained by the removed 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q=0} contribution and the integral is linear with the radius of the sphere (as shown in Appendix B.2), which is proportional to 1/Nq1/N_{q}.

IV.3 Increasing NqN_{q} does not lead to convergence

In the case of polar materials, when we consider the renormalization of a state at the VBM or the CBM, the adiabatic equation diverges. Indeed,

VNq3​∑q1q2​(q2+i​δ)\frac{V}{N_{q}^{3}}\sum_{q}\frac{1}{q^{2}(q^{2}+i\delta)} (39)

diverges as NqN_{q}. An example of this case is given in the middle left Figure 16b for the VBM of boron nitride using the adiabatic equation.

More specifically, neglecting the q=0q=0 contribution in the numerical integration of Eq. (39) gives a convergence behavior that can be modeled by the spherical integration of the summand of Eq. (39) in a shell from qc/Nqq_{c}/N_{q} to qcq_{c}. This gives, for δ=0\delta=0

∫−ππd​ϕ​∫0πd​θ​∫qc/Nqqcd​q​1q4\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\phi\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta\int_{q_{c}/N_{q}}^{q_{c}}dq\frac{1}{q^{4}} =4​π​∫qc/Nqqcd​q​1q2\displaystyle=4\pi\int_{q_{c}/N_{q}}^{q_{c}}dq\frac{1}{q^{2}}
=4​π​(1qc−1qc/Nq).\displaystyle=4\pi\left(\frac{1}{q_{c}}-\frac{1}{q_{c}/N_{q}}\right). (40)

As 1/Nq1/N_{q} goes to 0, the value of this integral indeed diverges linearly with the number of division NqN_{q}. This shows that, for polar materials, only the non-adiabatic equation can be safely used.

V Behavior of the i​δi\delta convergences

After enforcing the charge neutrality by application of Eq. (26), the theoretical rate of convergence of the ZPR can be analyzed when the small imaginary parameter i​δi\delta tends to 0. After isolating the divergent behavior, we will analyze analytically, and numerically on simple models, the rate of convergence of the ZPR.

We will observe that the δ\delta convergence can be square-root, linear or Lorentzian-like, depending on the state that is renormalized, the use of the adiabatic or non-adiabatic equation as well as the fact that the material is polar or not. The table (3) gives a summary of those behavior.

V.1 Convergence proportional to the square-root of δ\delta

For a non-polar material at the VBM or CBM, in the adiabatic framework, we can determine the ZPR dependence on the (finite) δ\delta value by analytically integrating Eq. (37)

ℜ∭d3q1q2+i​δ\displaystyle\Re\iiint d^{3}q\frac{1}{q^{2}+i\delta} =4​π​∫0qcd​q​q4q4+δ2\displaystyle=4\pi\int_{0}^{q_{c}}dq\frac{q^{4}}{q^{4}+\delta^{2}}
=4​π​δ​∫0qcd​qδ​q4δ2q4δ2+1.\displaystyle=4\pi\sqrt{\delta}\int_{0}^{q_{c}}\frac{dq}{\sqrt{\delta}}\frac{\frac{q^{4}}{\delta^{2}}}{\frac{q^{4}}{\delta^{2}}+1}. (41)

Carrying the integration and making a Taylor expansion for small δqc\frac{\sqrt{\delta}}{q_{c}} yields

4​π​qc+4​π​C​δ+𝒪⁡(δ),4\pi q_{c}+4\pi C\sqrt{\delta}+\mathcal{O}(\delta), (42)

with CC a constant. This result matches the δ\sqrt{\delta} behavior observed in our numerical integration in the bottom of Figure 4.

V.2 Convergence proportional to δ\delta

V.2.1 Non-polar materials in the adiabatic and non-adiabatic approximation at a non-extremal point

For non-polar materials, when considering a 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point other than the VBM or CBM, the adiabatic equation can be modeled as

ℜ∭0qcd3q1ε⁡(𝐪)+i​δ,\Re\iiint_{0}^{q_{c}}d^{3}q\frac{1}{\varepsilon(\mathbf{q})+i\delta}, (43)

where we have defined ε⁡(𝐪)=ε𝐤+𝐪−ε𝐤\varepsilon(\mathbf{q})=\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}-\varepsilon_{\mathbf{k}}.

Since the small i​δi\delta will only affect the integrand around the pole at ε⁡(𝐪)=0\varepsilon(\mathbf{q})=0, we can determine the δ\delta dependence of this model ZPR by considering only a small range of energy η\eta around it. We can then re-write Eq. (43) as

∫−ηηd​E​g​(E)​f​(E),\int_{-\eta}^{\eta}dEg(E)f(E), (44)

with g⁡(E)≜∑𝐪δ⁡(E−ε⁡(𝐪))g(E)\triangleq\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\delta(E-\varepsilon(\mathbf{q})) the density of states and

f⁡(E)≜1E+i​δ.f(E)\triangleq\frac{1}{E+i\delta}. (45)

We can make a Taylor expansion of the density of states around E=0E=0 (since η\eta is small)

g⁡(E)=g⁡(0)+g′​(0)​E+𝒪⁡(E2).g(E)=g(0)+g^{\prime}(0)E+\mathcal{O}(E^{2}). (46)

The even terms in Eq. (46) will not contribute because ℜ⁡f⁡(E)\Re f(E) is an odd function, therefore making no contribution to the integral. Therefore, the leading term is the first-order one. The integral can thus be re-written as

δ​∫−ηηd​Eδ​g′​(0)​E2δ2E2δ2+1=2​δ​g′​(0)​(ηδ−tan−1⁡(ηδ)).\delta\int_{-\eta}^{\eta}\frac{dE}{\delta}\frac{g^{\prime}(0)\frac{E^{2}}{\delta^{2}}}{\frac{E^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+1}=2\delta g^{\prime}(0)\Big(\frac{\eta}{\delta}-\tan^{-1}(\frac{\eta}{\delta})\Big). (47)

Making a Taylor expansion of Eq. (47) for small δη\frac{\delta}{\eta} leads to

2​g′​(0)​η−δ​g′​(0)​π,2g^{\prime}(0)\eta-\delta g^{\prime}(0)\pi, (48)

where we can see that this function is linear in δ\delta.

In the framework of the non-adiabatic theory, the integral is changed to

∫d​E​f​(E+ω)​g​(E).\int dEf(E+\omega)g(E). (49)

As this function has poles when E=−ωE=-\omega, we will now integrate around −ω-\omega

∫−ω−η−ω+ηd​E​f​(E+ω)​g​(E)\int_{-\omega-\eta}^{-\omega+\eta}dEf(E+\omega)g(E) (50)

After the change of variable u=E+ωu=E+\omega, we obtain

∫−ηηd​u​f​(u)​g​(u−ω)\int_{-\eta}^{\eta}duf(u)g(u-\omega) (51)

The density of states can again be Taylor expanded around −ω-\omega, giving

g⁡(u−ω)=g⁡(−ω)+u​g′​(−ω)+𝒪⁡(u2).g(u-\omega)=g(-\omega)+ug^{\prime}(-\omega)+\mathcal{O}(u^{2}). (52)

The same steps that led us from Eq. (46) to Eq. (48) now give us

2​g′​(−ω)​η−δ​g′​(−ω)​π,2g^{\prime}(-\omega)\eta-\delta g^{\prime}(-\omega)\pi, (53)

which is again linear in δ\delta.

In conclusion, the behavior of the ZPR of non-polar materials for non-extremum 𝐤\mathbf{k}-points in the BZ is linear when δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0.

V.2.2 Polar materials in the adiabatic and non-adiabatic approximation at a non-extremal point

For polar materials, we can use the shifted parabola model (defined in Eq. (35)) in Eq. (43), multiply the integrand by 1q2\frac{1}{q^{2}} and for the non-adiabatic framework, add ω\omega to i​δi\delta. Within this model, it is possible to show (see Appendix B.3) that, for small δ\delta, the ZPR converges linearly with δ\delta. In practice, the value that is reached by the linear regime is very high and tends to infinity at VBM or CBM.

V.3 Convergence in δ\delta proportional to a Lorentzian

V.3.1 Non-polar materials in the non-adiabatic approximation at the VBM/CBM

When considering the non-adiabatic equation at the VBM or CBM of a non-polar material, the ZPR behavior with respect to δ\delta is

ℜ∭d3q1q2+ω+i​δ=4πℜ∫0qcdqq2q2+ω+i​δ,\Re\iiint d^{3}q\frac{1}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta}=4\pi\Re\int_{0}^{q_{c}}dq\frac{q^{2}}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta}, (54)

which gives

4​π​ℜ⁡(qc−ω+i​δ​tan−1⁡(qcω+i​δ))4\pi\Re\Big(q_{c}-\sqrt{\omega+i\delta}\tan^{-1}\Big(\frac{q_{c}}{\sqrt{\omega+i\delta}}\Big)\Big) (55)

Plotting Eq. (55) reveals a Lorentzian-like shape centered at δ=0\delta=0. This can also be seen in the δ\delta-dependence of the numerical integration of Eq. (54)

1Nq3​∑Sqc(q2+ω)(q2+ω)2+δ2,\frac{1}{N_{q}^{3}}\sum_{S_{q_{c}}}\frac{(q^{2}+\omega)}{(q^{2}+\omega)^{2}+\delta^{2}}, (56)

where SqcS_{q_{c}} is a sphere of radius qcq_{c}. This dependence is shown at the bottom of Figure 3 for a cutoff radius qc=0.5q_{c}=0.5 and ω=0.01\omega=0.01.

In practice, we also observe that non-adiabatic ZPR for VBM/CBM of non-polar materials can be accurately fitted by a Lorentzian function. We thus use this type of functional dependence of the ZPR in δ\delta to extrapolate the results at δ=0\delta=0.

V.3.2 Polar materials in the non-adiabatic approximation at the VBM/CBM

For polar materials, we get a supplementary 1q2\frac{1}{q^{2}} factor in the integrand of Eq. (54), which thus becomes

ℜ∭d3q1q21q2+ω+i​δ=4​π​ℜ​∫0∞d​q​1q2+ω+i​δ,\Re\iiint d^{3}q\frac{1}{q^{2}}\frac{1}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta}\\ =4\pi\Re\int_{0}^{\infty}dq\frac{1}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta}, (57)

which becomes

2​π​ℜ​∫−∞∞d​q​1q2+ω+i​δ.2\pi\Re\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dq\frac{1}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta}. (58)

This integral can be performed by closing the contour of integration using a half-circle of infinite radius in the upper complex plane (which does not contribute to the integral) and then using the residue theorem. We obtain

2​π​ℜ​∫−∞∞d​q​1q2+ω+i​δ=2​π2​1ω​(1+(δω)2)14​ℜ⁡e−i2​tan−1⁡(δω),2\pi\Re\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}dq\frac{1}{q^{2}+\omega+i\delta}\\ =2\pi^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\omega}\big(1+(\frac{\delta}{\omega})^{2}\big)^{\frac{1}{4}}}\Re e^{-\frac{i}{2}\tan^{-1}(\frac{\delta}{\omega})}, (59)

which gives

2​π2​1ω​(1+(δω)2)14​cos⁡(12​tan−1⁡(δω)).2\pi^{2}\frac{1}{\sqrt{\omega}\big(1+(\frac{\delta}{\omega})^{2}\big)^{\frac{1}{4}}}\cos\Big(\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\big(\frac{\delta}{\omega}\big)\Big). (60)

Plotting Eq. (60) again reveals a Lorentzian-like shape centered at δ=0\delta=0. Accordingly, fitting the results using a Lorentzian is also found to be a good approximation in practice for polar materials.

V.4 Decreasing δ\delta does not lead to convergence

The adiabatic ZPR for the VBM/CBM of a polar material has already been shown to diverge with increasing 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point sampling (see subsection IV.3). We now examine the δ\delta-dependence of the ZPR, which has the form

ℜ∭d3q1q2​(q2+i​δ)\displaystyle\Re\iiint d^{3}q\frac{1}{q^{2}(q^{2}+i\delta)} =4​π​ℜ​∫0qcd​q​1q2+i​δ\displaystyle=4\pi\Re\int_{0}^{q_{c}}dq\frac{1}{q^{2}+i\delta}
=4​πδ​∫0qcd​qδ​q2δq4δ2+1.\displaystyle=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{\delta}}\int_{0}^{q_{c}}\frac{dq}{\sqrt{\delta}}\frac{\frac{q^{2}}{\delta}}{\frac{q^{4}}{\delta^{2}}+1}. (61)

When qc/δq_{c}/\sqrt{\delta} is rather large (i.e. >10>10), which happens for small δ\delta, the integral of Eq. (61) converges logarithmically to its value at infinity and we obtain 2​π2δ\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi^{2}}{\sqrt{\delta}}.

We therefore see that Eq. (61) will numerically diverge as 1δ\frac{1}{\sqrt{\delta}} for small values of δ\delta. An example of this kind of divergence is given in the middle right of Figure 9 of supplemental materials [22] for the VBM of β\beta-AlN (a polar material) using the adiabatic equation.

VI Results on different semiconductors

We will now examine five different semiconductors, two of which are non polar materials (diamond and silicon), and three of which are polar materials (α\alpha-AlN, β\beta-AlN and BN). We will be able to provide fully converged results, independent of any arbitrary parameter, like an ad hoc broadening parameter. Of course, as outlined previously, in the case of polar materials, only the non-adiabatic theory can provide such results, as the standard adiabatic AHC theory breaks down for these.

VI.1 Non polar materials

VI.1.1 Diamond

Diamond is a metastable allotrope of carbon where the C atoms are arranged into two interpenetrating face-centered cubic lattices shifted along the body diagonal by 14th\frac{1}{4}^{\text{th}} of its length. The space group associated with this spatial arrangement is Fd3¯\bar{3}m (cubic, 227). Diamond has the highest hardness and thermal conductivity of any bulk material [23]. It is therefore used as cutting and polishing tool in the industry. Even though the stable phase of bulk carbon under normal condition is graphite, we will focus on the diamond phase.

The pseudopotential was generated using the fhi98PP code [42] with a 1.5 atomic unit cut-off radius for pseudization. The valence electrons of carbon, treated explicitly in the ab-initio calculations, are the 2s22p23d0 orbitals.

Careful convergence studies (error below 0.5 mHa per atom on the total energy) led to the use of a 6x6x6 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-centered Monkhorst-Pack 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point sampling [43] of the BZ and an energy cut-off of 30 Hartree for the truncation of the plane wave basis set. The Perdew and Zunger parametrization of LDA [44] was used. The relaxed lattice parameter is calculated to be 6.652 Bohr, 1.3% below the experimental value of 6.740 Bohr, measured at room temperature [39] (see Table 4 for more information on the structural properties).

The electronic bandstructure was computed at the DFT level and gave a direct bandgap at 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma} of 5.67 eV and an indirect 𝚪−0.727​𝐗\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-0.727\mathbf{X} bandgap of 4.25 eV, intrinsically below the experimental bandgap of 5.48 eV at 0 K [45](see Table 5).

For the calculations of the ZPR, we used 10 bands to describe the active space in Eqs. (15) and (16).

The convergences with respect to 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point integration for the band edges and the direct band gap of diamond are shown on Figure 5a, where the densest used grid is a 125x125x125 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid (43680 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points in the irreducible Brillouin-Zone (IBZ)). The Γ15c\Gamma_{15}^{c} state is not the bottom of the conduction band, and therefore there are other states in the BZ with close energy. This leads to numerical instabilities as the denominator of the adiabatic Eq. (15) can diverge for small i​δi\delta. For large enough imaginary component, the ZPR converges to approximatively -270 meV. The top of the valence band Γ25v\Gamma_{25}^{v} converges linearly and can be extrapolated to infinitely dense 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid. To obtain a definite value for the ZPR, we have to converge the ZPR for vanishing δ\delta. The convergence can be found on Figure (5b) and shows that large 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid are required to enter the expected linear regime (see section V.2 for more information). The extrapolated ZPR is -277.61 meV. The VBM can be smoothly extrapolated using a square-root fit to zero value of δ\delta to give 160.96 meV. The adiabatic direct bandgap ZPR of diamond is computed to be -438.6 meV.

For the non-adiabatic direct bandgap of diamond, the convergence can be found on Figure 6 and shows that the Γ15c\Gamma_{15}^{c} state converges similarly but the VBM has a rapid convergence in 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point integration and a Lorentzian behavior for the δ\delta extrapolation. The fitted Lorentzian have three fitting parameters: a multiplicative constant AA, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) and an additive constant BB

A​Γ2​π(Γ2)2+x2+B,A\frac{\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi}}{(\frac{\Gamma}{2})^{2}+x^{2}}+B, (62)

where here A=10.11A=10.11, Γ=0.55\Gamma=0.55 and B=121.90B=121.90. The extrapolated ZPR is of -283.23 meV and 133.57 meV for the Γ15c\Gamma_{15}^{c} and Γ25v\Gamma_{25}^{v} states, respectively. This leads to a reduction of -415.8 meV of the direct bandgap due to electron-phonon interaction at 0 K.

The convergences of the CBM for diamond are given in Figures 1 and 2 of the supplemental materials [22] using the adiabatic and non-adiabatic equations, respectively. For the adiabatic case, the fact that the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-convergence is not smooth for relatively small i​δi\delta is due to the finite 𝐤+𝐪\mathbf{k+q} sampling. Indeed, when we compute the renormalization at one of the 6 symmetry equivalent CBM 𝐤\mathbf{k}-points, the 𝐤+𝐪\mathbf{k+q} sampling is such that the other five equivalent 𝐤\mathbf{k}-points are not sampled exactly (not the numerically accurate minimum). The extrapolated ZPR of the CBM state is -219.24 meV using a square root fit for the adiabatic equation and -196.22 meV using a Lorentzian fit for the non-adiabatic equation (see Table 6 for more information).

The temperature dependence of the direct and indirect bandgaps is reported on Figure 7 for a 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid and shows that the slope at high temperature for the non-adiabatic renormalization with a Lorentzian extrapolation to vanishing imaginary parameter δ\delta is -0.504 meV/K for the direct bandgap and -0.435 meV/K for the indirect one. The phonon-induced broadening 12​τn​𝐤(a​d​i​a​b​a​t​i​c,R​I​A)\frac{1}{2\tau_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(adiabatic,RIA)}} of Eq. (18) is calculated for the 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid to be 180 meV and 63 meV for the direct and indirect bandgap of diamond at 0 K, respectively.

Our result underestimates the experimental ZPR of the diamond indirect bandgap of -364 meV [59] by 9.4%. Since our calculation neglects several effects like anharmonicity, non-rigid-ion terms or many-body G​WGW corrections, we are rather close to the experimental value. The measured linear slope at high temperature for the indirect bandgap of diamond is -0.54 meV/K [59]. The measured linear slope at high temperature for the direct bandgap is −0.60-0.60 or −0.69-0.69 meV/K [58], depending on the analysis11 1 Logothetidis et al. deduced the temperature dependence of the direct bandgap of diamond from first and second-derivative line-shape analysis, see Ref. 58 for more details.. Our theoretical values for the indirect and direct bandgaps underestimate the experimental ones by 19% and 16%, respectively. We hypothesize that this underestimation of the linear slope at high temperature for the direct bandgap of diamond is due to the underestimation of the ZPR within DFT. Indeed, as discussed in Ref. 13, the correction brought by G​WGW to the ZPR is quite substantial for the direct bandgap (-209 meV). Since the ZPR is directly linked with the slope at high temperature, it is not surprising that we witness such an underestimation with respect to the experimental results. We did not compute such GW correction for ZPR of the indirect bandgap of diamond but expect from the results of Figure 7 to have a smaller correction.

It is worthwhile to note that the complete lack of experimental data for low temperature (T << 100 K) and the relatively large error bars (up to ±\pm10 meV) between 200 K and 350 K generate an uncertainty of several meV on the experimental ZPR [61]. This calls for new, reliable and wide range temperature measurement of the evolution of the bandgap with temperature in diamond. We hope that our theoretical study will stimulate such experimental interest.

Finally, the non-adiabatically renormalized electronic bandstructure of diamond at 0K along the 𝐋−𝚪−𝐗\mathbf{L}-\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-\mathbf{X} high symmetry line is shown on Figure 8 for a 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid for δ\delta extrapolated to zero linearly and with a Lorentzian for the VBM and CBM.

VI.1.2 Silicon

Silicon is a tetravalent metalloid widely used in integrated circuits and semiconductor electronics. It has a diamond cubic crystal structure with a Fd3¯\bar{3}m (cubic, 227) space group. Pure silicon is usually not found in nature but manufactured to get monocrystalline silicon for use in computer microchips. Although the manufacturing process is rather expensive, this material is so important that about 50.000 metric tons are produced per year worldwide [62].

The pseudopotential used for silicon was generated using the fhi98PP code [42] with a 1.0247 atomic unit cut-off radius for pseudization. The pseudopotential is a Troullier-Martins with the Perdew/Wang [63] parametrization of LDA. The valence electrons of silicon, treated explicitly in the ab-initio calculations, are the 3s23p2 orbitals.

Careful convergence checks (error below 0.5 mHa per atom on the total energy) lead to the use of a 6x6x6 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-centered Monkhorst-Pack 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point sampling [43] of the BZ and an energy cut-off of 20 Hartree for the truncation of the plane wave basis set. The relaxed lattice parameter is calculated to be 10.170 Bohr, 0.9% below the experimental value, measured at room temperature [41] (see Table 4 for more information on the structural properties).

The electronic bandstructure was computed at the DFT level and gave a direct gap at 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma} of 2.567 eV and an indirect 𝚪−0.848​𝐗\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-0.848\mathbf{X} bandgap of 0.463 eV intrinsically below the experimental bandgaps of 3.378 and 1.17 eV at ∼\sim10K [56] for the direct and indirect bandgap, respectively (see Table 5). Many ab-initio simulations have been performed on silicon and give similar values to ours. For example, Ref. 55 got a direct bandgap of 2.52 eV and an indirect one of 0.45 eV, also using the Abinit software.

For the calculations of the ZPR, we used 10 bands to describe the active space in Eqs. (15) and (16). The convergence with respect to 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point integration for the direct bandgaps of silicon is shown on Figure 3 of the supplemental materials [22] for the adiabatic equation and gives a linearly extrapolated ZPR of -6.23 meV for the Γ15c\Gamma_{15}^{c} state and a square-root extrapolation of 40.87 meV for the ZPR of the VBM, thus leading to a ZPR of -47.1 meV for the direct bandgap. The non-adiabatic direct bandgap ZPR shown on Figure 4 of the supplemental materials [22] of the Γ15c\Gamma_{15}^{c} state is calculated to be -7.36 meV and 34.87 meV for the VBM. The non-adiabatic bandgap ZPR is therefore slightly smaller than the adiabatic one with a value of -42.1 meV. The densest grid computed is a 100x100x100 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid (22776 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points in the IBZ). The convergences with respect to the indirect bandgap of silicon are shown in Figures 5 and 6 of the supplemental materials [22] for the adiabatic and non-adiabatic equations respectively. The ZPR of the first one can be extrapolated to -23.28 meV for the CBM and 40.87 meV for the VBM, leading to -64.3 meV renormalization of the bandgap. The second one can be extrapolated to -21.43 meV for the CBM and 34.75 meV for the VBM, leading to a smaller -56.2 meV renormalization of the bandgap.

Such values can be compared with those mentioned in the recently published paper by Patrick and Giustino [40] who obtain values of -57 and -22 meV for the indirect and direct bandgap renormalization of silicon using a 4x4x4 supercell within the AHC framework (adiabatic equation). Their results matches ours for the adiabatic 4x4x4 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid (1/Nq=0.251/N_{q}=0.25) with -52 and -29 meV for the indirect and direct bandgaps, respectively (as can also be seen on Figures 3 and 5 of the supplemental materials [22]).

The non-adiabatic temperature dependence of direct and indirect 𝚪−0.848​𝐗\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-0.848\mathbf{X} bandgaps integrated over a 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid with a Lorentzian extrapolation to vanishing imaginary parameter δ\delta is reported on Figure 9 and gives slopes at high temperature of −0.147-0.147 and −0.255-0.255 meV/K, respectively.

The experimental zero-point motion renormalization of the silicon indirect bandgap is −62-62 meV obtained from mass derivative of the gap or −64-64 meV obtained from linear extrapolation to 0 K [59]. The measured linear slope at high temperature is −0.32-0.32 meV/K [64, 65]. Those experimental results are larger than our theoretical ones using the non-adiabatic extension to the AHC equations, as expected from DFT calculations. This is linked with the fact that we underestimate the ZPR with respect to GW calculations.

Additionally, we present on Figure 10 the phonon-induced broadening of the direct and indirect bandgap of silicon with temperature. The direct and indirect bandgap broadening at 0 K are computed to be 31 meV and 23 meV, respectively. The experimental broadening, measured with spectroscopic ellipsometry in Ref. 66 (red dots), is attributed to the broadening of the E1=𝚲3v−𝚲1c\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{3}^{v}-\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{1}^{c} direct transition with temperature. In Ref. 66, it is also mentioned that the measured values at higher temperature (black dots) are difficult to attribute to the broadening of one particular transition because the E1 gap is nearly degenerate with the E0′=𝚪25′v−𝚪15c{}_{0}^{\prime}=\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{25^{\prime}}^{v}-\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{15}^{c}. Since the ellipsometry measurement is a spectroscopic measurement, it can only probe direct transitions. In consequence, we should compare the broadening results (both black and red dots) with the silicon red line (direct-gap E′0{}_{0}^{\prime}).

Finally, the non-adiabatically renormalized electronic bandstructure of silicon at 0 K along the 𝐋−𝚪−𝐗\mathbf{L}-\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-\mathbf{X} high symmetry line is shown on Figure 11 for a 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid with δ\delta extrapolated to zero.

VI.2 Polar materials

VI.2.1 Aluminum Nitride

Aluminum nitride in the wurtzite structure (α\alpha-AlN) is one of the widest bandgap nitride semiconductor. It has a P63mc (hexagonal, 186) space group. α\alpha-AlN is used for high-temperature electronics and opto-electronic applications [48] with a melting temperature of 3273 K [67]. The zincblende form of aluminum nitride (β\beta-AlN) has a F4¯​3\bar{4}3m (cubic, 216) space group and has been reported to be experimentally metastable [27]. We will study the temperature-dependence properties of these two phases using the equations mentioned above to compute the ZPR.

Concerning the numerical details of the calculations, the aluminium and nitrogen pseudopotentials were generated using the fhi98PP code [42] with a 1.0247 atomic unit cut-off radius for pseudization and a maximum angular channel of l=2l=2. Both of them are Troullier-Martins pseudopotentials with the Perdew/Wang [63] parametrization of LDA. The valence electrons of aluminum and nitrogen, treated explicitly in the ab-initio calculations, are generated for the 3s23p1 and 2s22p3 configuration, respectively.

Convergence checks (error below 0.5 mHa per atom on the total energy) lead to the use of a 6x6x6 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-centered Monkhorst-Pack 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point sampling [43] of the BZ and an energy cut-off of 35 Hartree for the truncation of the plane wave basis set.

The relaxed lattice parameters are calculated to be a=5.783 and c=9.255 Bohr for α\alpha-AlN and a=8.130 Bohr for β\beta-AlN. These values are at maximum 2.3% below the experimental one (see Table 4).

The electronic bandstructures were computed at the LDA level. For α\alpha-AlN, there is a direct gap at 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma} of 4.691 eV. This is well above the 4.056 eV bandgap computed within the Material’s Project using GGA [25] but well in the range of other LDA bandgaps (see Table 5). These DFT values naturally underestimate the experimental bandgap of 6.28 eV at 5K [47, 49]. The zincblende β\beta-AlN turns out to have an indirect 𝚪−𝐗\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-\mathbf{X} bandgap of 3.308 eV, almost identical to the Materials Project value (see Table 5). The direct gap at 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma} of 4.677 eV is a bit above most the the LDA values reported in the Table. We have nonetheless to bear in mind that the 4.2 eV LDA direct gap calculation performed in Ref. 48 is done at the experimental lattice parameter.

For the calculations of the ZPR we used 18 bands to describe the active space in Eqs. (15) and (16).

The 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point integration for the direct bandgaps of α\alpha-AlN is shown on Figure 7 of the supplemental materials [22] for the adiabatic equation and diverges for dense 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid as AlN is a polar material. The non-adiabatic direct bandgap ZPR shown on Figure 8 of the supplemental materials [22] converges linearly with the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid and the δ\delta behavior can be fitted by a Lorentzian function to 0. It gives a ZPR of -183.5 meV for the CBM and 194.2 meV for the VBM, leading to a ZPR of the direct bandgap of α\alpha-AlN of -377.7 meV. The densest grid computed is a 34x34x34 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid (2052 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points in the IBZ).

For the same reason as α\alpha-AlN, the β\beta-AlN diverges for the adiabatic equation and the divergence is shown on Figures 9 and 11 of the supplemental materials [22]. The non-adiabatic direct bandgap ZPR shown on Figure 10 of the supplemental materials [22] converges linearly with the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid and the δ\delta behavior can be fitted by a linear or Lorentzian function to 0. It gives a ZPR of -187.54 meV for the CBM and 226.08 meV for the VBM, thus leading to a ZPR of the direct bandgap of β\beta-AlN of -413.62 meV. The non-adiabatic indirect bandgap ZPR of β\beta-AlN is shown on Figure 12 of the supplemental materials [22] and converges linearly with the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid and the δ\delta behavior can be fitted by a Lorentzian function to 0. This results into a ZPR of -108.36 meV for the CBM, resulting in a -334.4 meV ZPR of the indirect bandgap of β\beta-AlN (see Table 6 for more information). The densest computed grid is a 100x100x1000 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid ( 22776 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points in the IBZ).

The temperature dependence of the three gaps is reported on Figures 12 and 13. The linear slopes at high temperature can be extracted to be -0.772, -0.521 and -0.763 meV/K for the direct gap of α\alpha-AlN, the indirect bandgap of β\beta-AlN and the direct bandgap of β\beta-AlN, respectively.

The phonon-induced broadening is calculated for the 34x34x34 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid to be 117 meV for the direct bandgap of α\alpha-AlN. The broadening of the direct and indirect bandgaps of β\beta-AlN at 0 K integrated on a 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid are 118 meV and 108 meV, respectively.

The experimental ZPR for α\alpha-AlN has been obtained from linear extrapolation to 0 K of the change of the direct bandgap with temperature and yield a value of -239 meV with a linear slope at high temperature of -0.83 meV/K [68, 61, 59], in relatively good agreement with our -​0.772\text{-}0.772 meV/K value. The obvious disagreement with our theoretical value for the direct bandgap ZPR (-369 meV versus -239 meV) can be attributed to the fact that the experimental data set measured by Brunner et al. [68] are very scarce and on a narrow temperature range (4-298 K). As pointed out by Pässler [61] for this compounds: “this illustrates the great importance of extending experimental measurements in wide bandgap materials far beyond room temperature”.

Finally, we show in Figures 14 and 15 the non-adiabaticly renormalized electronic bandstructure at 0 K along the highest symmetry 𝚪−𝐌\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-\mathbf{M} path for α\alpha-AlN and along the 𝐋−𝚪−𝐗\mathbf{L}-\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-\mathbf{X} path of the β\beta phase of AlN. The thickness of the lines is associated with the lifetime of the electronic state computed with Eq. (18).

VI.2.2 Boron Nitride

Boron nitride (BN) exists in various crystalline forms. Its most stable phase under normal condition is an hexagonal layered arrangement. It used as a lubricant and an additive to cosmetic products. The cubic boron nitride (c-BN) has a zincblende structure and is isoelectronic to diamond. It is the second hardest material below diamond, but its chemical stability is far superior with high thermal conductivity and low dielectric constant [70]. Boron nitride is not found in nature and is therefore produced synthetically from boric acid or boron trioxide. We will only study the c-BN polymorph here.

The boron and nitrogen pseudopotentials were also generated using the fhi98PP code [42] with a 1.0247 atomic unit cut-off radius for pseudization and a maximum angular channel of l=2l=2. Both of them are Troullier-Martins pseudopotential with the Perdew/Wang [63] parametrization of LDA. The valence electrons of boron and nitrogen, treated explicitly in the ab-initio calculations, are the 2s22p1 and 2s22p3 orbitals, respectively.

Careful convergence checks (error below 0.5 mHa per atom on the total energy) lead to the use of a 8x8x8 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-centered Monkhorst-Pack 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point sampling [43] of the BZ and an energy cut-off of 35 Hartree for the truncation of the plane wave basis set.

The relaxed lattice parameter is calculated to be 6.746 Bohr, 1.3% below the experimental value of 6.833 Bohr [33] (see Table 4 for more information on the structural properties).

The electronic bandstructure was computed at the DFT level and gave a direct gap at 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma} of 8.890 eV and an indirect 𝚪−𝐗\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-\mathbf{X} bandgap of 4.446 eV, intrinsically below the experimental bandgap of 6.4 eV at 300K [54] (see Table 5). For the calculations of the ZPR, we used 18 bands to describe the active space in Eqs. (15) and (16).

The c-BN is also a polar material and therefore diverges for the adiabatic equation as shown on Figures 16 and 14 of the supplemental materials [22]. The non-adiabatic direct bandgap ZPR shown on Figure 13 of the supplemental materials [22] converges linearly with the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid and the δ\delta behavior can be fitted by a linear or Lorentzian function to 0 and gives a ZPR of -301.48 meV for the Γ1c\Gamma_{1}^{c} state and 200.5 meV for the VBM, thus leading to a ZPR of the direct bandgap of c-BN of -502.0 meV. The non-adiabatic indirect bandgap ZPR of c-BN is shown on Figure 15 of the supplemental materials [22] and converges linearly with the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid and the δ\delta behavior can be fitted by a Lorentzian function to 0 and gives a ZPR of -205.08 meV for the CBM, thus leading to a ZPR of the indirect bandgap of c-BN of -405.6 meV (see Table 6 for more information). The densest grid computed is a 100x100x1000 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid ( 22776 𝐪\mathbf{q}-points in the IBZ).

The non-adiabatic temperature dependence of direct and indirect bandgaps are reported on Figure 17 for a 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid with extrapolation to zero δ\delta and give slopes at high temperature of -0.639 and -0.521 meV/K, respectively. The phonon-induced broadening is calculated for the 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grid to be 315 meV and 136 meV for the direct and indirect bandgap of c-BN at 0 K, respectively.

Finally, the non-adiabatic renormalized electronic bandstructure of c-BN at 0K along the 𝐋−𝚪−𝐗\mathbf{L}-\boldsymbol{\Gamma}-\mathbf{X} high symmetry line is shown on Figure 18 for a 75x75x75 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point grid with δ\delta extrapolated to zero.

VII Conclusions

After a brief reminder of the theory, we present a solution to the divergence problem due to a residual Born effective charge stemming from the finite 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point grid in numerical ab-initio calculations. We analyze theoretically the 𝐪\mathbf{q}-point convergence for a polar or non-polar material; in the adiabatic or non-adiabatic approximation; for the renormalization of the band extrema or other states. We propose an equivalent analysis for the convergence of the imaginary parameter δ\delta tending to zero. We demonstrate that the adiabatic AHC formalism breaks down for polar materials and the non-adiabatic AHC formalism should therefore be used for these materials. We then propose a systematic procedure to converge the zero-point motion renormalization (ZPR) and apply it for five semiconductors and insulators (diamond, silicon, the α\alpha and β\beta phase of aluminum nitride and boron nitride). For these materials, we present the non-adiabatic renormalized electronic bandstructure (at the density functional theory level) due to electron-phonon coupling as well as the phonon induced lifetime in the adiabatic limit. We also show the temperature dependence of their direct and indirect bandgaps and compare them with experiment whenever available. The non-adiabatic ZPR at the DFT level systematically underestimates the experimental results (by less than 10%) except in α\alpha-AlN where the theoretical value is larger than the experimental one. We strongly question the validity of the experimental result in this case as the experimental ZPR was obtained by linear extrapolation to 0 K on a very limited temperature range (0-300 K) where the linear regime was not yet achieved. We therefore believe that the experimental result for α\alpha-AlN from Ref. 68 is underestimated. On the one hand, we hope that our work will emulate experimental work on wider temperature range. On the other hand, this approach might also be used in the future to compute more evolved temperature-dependent properties depending on the electronic structure, as e.g. optical properties.
