Appendix A Derivation of the renormalization factor

A.1 Minimization of the variational second-order electronic energy

The variational second-order electronic energy without non-linear core correction can be written as (see Eq. (60) of Ref. 20)

E−𝐪,𝐪(2)=Ω0(2​π)3​∫B​Zd​𝐤​∑no​c​csn​(⟨un​𝐤,𝐪(1)|H𝐤+𝐪,𝐤+𝐪(0)−εn​𝐤(0)|un​𝐤,𝐪(1)⟩+⟨un​𝐤,𝐪(1)|ve​x​t,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)​|un​𝐤(0)⟩+⟨un​𝐤(0)|​ve​x​t,𝐤,𝐤+𝐪(1)|un​𝐤,𝐪(1)⟩CLOSE+⟨un​𝐤(0)|ve​x​t,𝐤,𝐤(2)|un​𝐤(0)⟩)+12∫Ω0d2​(n​εx​c)d​n2|n(0)​(𝐫)|n𝐪(1)(𝐫)|2d𝐫+2πΩ0∑𝐆≠0|n𝐪(1)​(𝐆)|2|𝐪+𝐆|2+n𝐪(1)∗(𝐆=0)2​πqw𝐪(1)+n𝐪(1)(𝐆=0)2​πqw𝐪(1)∗+2πΩ0|n𝐪(1)​(𝐆=0)|2q2,E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{(2)}=\frac{\Omega_{0}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{BZ}d\mathbf{k}\sum_{n}^{occ}s_{n}\Big(\langle u_{n\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}|H_{\mathbf{k+q,k+q}}^{(0)}-\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|u_{n\mathbf{k,q}}^{(1)}\rangle+\langle u_{n\mathbf{k,q}}^{(1)}|v_{ext,\mathbf{k+q,k}}^{(1)}|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}\rangle+\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|v_{ext,\mathbf{k,k+q}}^{(1)}|u_{n\mathbf{k,q}}^{(1)}\rangle\\ +\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|v_{ext,\mathbf{k,k}}^{(2)}|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}\rangle\Big)+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega_{0}}\frac{d^{2}(n\varepsilon_{xc})}{dn^{2}}\bigg|_{n^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})}|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}d\mathbf{r}+2\pi\Omega_{0}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq 0}\frac{|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G})|^{2}}{|\mathbf{q+G}|^{2}}+n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)*}(\mathbf{G}=0)\frac{2\pi}{q}w_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}\\ +n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G}=0)\frac{2\pi}{q}w_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)*}+2\pi\Omega_{0}\frac{|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G}=0)|^{2}}{q^{2}}, (63)

where we follow the notation of Ref. 20, i.e. the superscripts (0)(0) and (1)(1) refer to the unperturbed and first-order perturbation (here in nucleus motion) of the periodic part of the wavefunction, sns_{n} is the spin degeneracy factor, ve​x​t,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)v_{ext,\mathbf{k+q},\mathbf{k}}^{(1)} is the first-order perturbed potential external to the electronic system that includes the nucleus one

ve​x​t,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)=vs​e​p,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)+v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1),v_{ext,\mathbf{k+q,k}}^{(1)}=v_{sep,\mathbf{k+q,k}}^{(1)}+\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}, (64)

and εx​c\varepsilon_{xc} is the exchange-correlation energy per electron

d2​(n​εx​c)d​n2|n(0)=d​vx​cd​n|n(0).\frac{d^{2}(n\varepsilon_{xc})}{dn^{2}}\bigg|_{n^{(0)}}=\frac{dv_{xc}}{dn}\bigg|_{n^{(0)}}. (65)

The second-order change of the nonlocal potential vs​e​p,𝐤,𝐤(2)v_{sep,\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}}^{(2)} is given in Eq. (54) of Ref. 20.

The first-order change of the local potential of Eq. (23) for 𝐆=0\mathbf{G}=0 can be written as

limq→0v¯l​o​c,𝐪(1)​(0)=4​πΩ0​1q​w𝐪(1),\lim_{q\to 0}\bar{v}_{loc,\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(0)=\frac{4\pi}{\Omega_{0}}\frac{1}{q}w_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}, (66)

with

w𝐪(1)=−iqαqe−i𝐪⋅𝝉κ(−Zκ+q24​πCκ+O(q4)).w_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}=-i\frac{q_{\alpha}}{q}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\kappa}}\Big(-Z_{\kappa}+\frac{q^{2}}{4\pi}C_{\kappa}+O(q^{4})\Big). (67)

To write Eq. (63) is a more compact form, we define the following vectors

𝐱i\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{i} ≜⟨𝐆|un​𝐤,𝐪(1)⟩\displaystyle\triangleq\braket{\mathbf{G}|u_{n\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}} (68)
𝐮i\displaystyle\mathbf{u}_{i} ≜sn​wn​𝐤​⟨𝐆|un​𝐤(0)⟩\displaystyle\triangleq s_{n}w_{n\mathbf{k}}\braket{\mathbf{G}|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}} (69)
𝐰i\displaystyle\mathbf{w}_{i} ≜sn​wn​𝐤​⟨𝐆|ve​x​t,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)|un​𝐤(0)⟩\displaystyle\triangleq s_{n}w_{n\mathbf{k}}\braket{\mathbf{G}|v_{ext,\mathbf{k+q},\mathbf{k}}^{(1)}|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}} (70)

where wn​𝐤w_{n\mathbf{k}} is the weight of the 𝐤\mathbf{k}-point and includes a band nn dependence to indicate that it is zero for unoccupied states and where the index ii stands for the combined planewave component 𝐆\mathbf{G}, band index nn and wave-vector 𝐤\mathbf{k} indices. It will later be useful to note that

𝐮†​𝐱=Ω0(2​π)3​∫B​Zd​𝐤​∑no​c​cs⁡⟨un​𝐤(0)|un​𝐤,𝐪(1)⟩=Ω02​n𝐪(1)​(𝐆=0).\begin{split}\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}&=\frac{\Omega_{0}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{BZ}d\mathbf{k}\sum_{n}^{occ}s\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|u_{n\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}\rangle\\ &=\frac{\Omega_{0}}{2}n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G}=0).\end{split} (71)

In addition, we define the following scalars

a\displaystyle a ≜8​πΩ0​1q2,\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{8\pi}{\Omega_{0}}\frac{1}{q^{2}}, (72)
b\displaystyle b ≜4​πΩ0​q​w𝐪(1),\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{4\pi}{\Omega_{0}q}w_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}, (73)
c\displaystyle c ≜Ω0(2​π)3​∫B​Zd​𝐤​∑no​c​csn​⟨un​𝐤(0)|ve​x​t,𝐤,𝐤(2)|un​𝐤(0)⟩.\displaystyle\triangleq\frac{\Omega_{0}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{BZ}d\mathbf{k}\sum_{n}^{occ}s_{n}\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|v_{ext,\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}}^{(2)}|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}\rangle. (74)

Finally, we introduce the matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} so that

𝐱†​𝐀𝐱≜Ω0(2​π)3​∫B​Zd​𝐤​∑no​c​csn​⟨un​𝐤,𝐪(1)|​H𝐤+𝐪,𝐤+𝐪(0)−εn​𝐤(0)​|un​𝐤,𝐪(1)⟩+12​∫Ω0d2​(n​εx​c)d​n2|n(0)​(𝐫)​|n𝐪(1)​(𝐫)|2​𝐝𝐫+2πΩ0∑𝐆≠0|n𝐪(1)​(𝐆)|2|𝐪+𝐆|2.\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}\triangleq\frac{\Omega_{0}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{BZ}d\mathbf{k}\sum_{n}^{occ}s_{n}\langle u_{n\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}|H_{\mathbf{k+q,k+q}}^{(0)}\\ -\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|u_{n\mathbf{k,q}}^{(1)}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega_{0}}\frac{d^{2}(n\varepsilon_{xc})}{dn^{2}}\bigg|_{n^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})}|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}d\mathbf{r}\\ +2\pi\Omega_{0}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq 0}\frac{|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G})|^{2}}{|\mathbf{q+G}|^{2}}. (75)

Using the above definitions (Eqs. (68)-(70) and (72)-(75)), Eq. (63) can be re-written in short-hand notation

E−𝐪,𝐪(2)=𝐱†​𝐀𝐱+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱)​(𝐱†​𝐮)+(b𝐱†𝐮+𝐱†𝐰+(c.c.))+c.E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{(2)}=\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{u})\\ +(b\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{w}+(c.c.))+c. (76)

The physical value of the first-order perturbed periodic part of the wavefunction 𝐱\mathbf{x} is the one that minimizes E−𝐪,𝐪(2)E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{(2)} (we will refer to it as 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1})

δ​E−𝐪,𝐪(2)=({δ​𝐱1†​(𝐀𝐱1+(b+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱1))​𝐮+𝐰)}CLOSE+(c.c.))=0.\delta E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{(2)}=(\{\delta\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_{1}+(b+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1}))\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w})\}\\ +(c.c.))=0. (77)

The real part of the quantity between curly bracket {} is therefore zero

ℜ⁡{δ​𝐱1†​(𝐀𝐱1+(b+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱1))​𝐮+𝐰)}=0.\Re\{\delta\mathbf{x}_{1}^{\dagger}\!(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_{1}+(b+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1}))\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w})\}=0. (78)

For the preceding relation to hold for any δ​𝐱\delta\mathbf{x}, the quantity in parenthesis () must be zero,

𝐀𝐱1+(b+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱1))​𝐮+𝐰=0,\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_{1}+(b+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1}))\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}=0, (79)

which leads to

𝐱1=−(b+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱1))​𝐀−1​𝐮−𝐀−1​𝐰.\mathbf{x}_{1}=-(b+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1}))\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{w}. (80)

We define

𝐱1≜𝐱1​a+𝐱1​b,\mathbf{x}_{1}\triangleq\mathbf{x}_{1a}+\mathbf{x}_{1b}, (81)

where

𝐱1​a≜−𝐀−1​𝐰,\mathbf{x}_{1a}\triangleq-\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{w}, (82)

and we are left with

𝐱1​b=−(b+a⁡(𝐮†​(𝐱1​a+𝐱1​b)))​𝐀−1​𝐮.\mathbf{x}_{1b}=-(b+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!(\mathbf{x}_{1a}+\mathbf{x}_{1b})))\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}. (83)

By defining

b′=b+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱1​a),b^{\prime}=b+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1a}), (84)

Eq. (83) becomes

𝐱1​b=−(b′+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱1​b))​𝐀−1​𝐮.\mathbf{x}_{1b}=-(b^{\prime}+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1b}))\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}. (85)

By multiplying the preceding equation by 𝐮†\mathbf{u}^{\dagger} and isolating 𝐮†​𝐱1​b\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1b}, we obtain

𝐮†​𝐱1​b=−b′​𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮1+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮).\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1b}=\frac{-b^{\prime}\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}}{1+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u})}. (86)

Substituting this result back in Eq. (85), we obtain 𝐱1​b\mathbf{x}_{1b}

𝐱1​b=−b′1+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮)​𝐀−1​𝐮,\mathbf{x}_{1b}=\frac{-b^{\prime}}{1+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u})}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}, (87)

and, using Eqs. (81), (82), and (84), we finally have

𝐱1=−𝐀−1​𝐰+−b+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐰)1+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮)​𝐀−1​𝐮.\mathbf{x}_{1}=-\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{w}+\frac{-b+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{w})}{1+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u})}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}. (88)

Substituting Eq. (79) into Eq. (76), we obtain the value of E−𝐪,𝐪(2)E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{(2)} at the minimum 𝐱1\mathbf{x}_{1}

E~−𝐪,𝐪(2)=b∗​𝐮†​𝐱1+𝐰†​𝐱1+c.\tilde{E}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{(2)}=b^{*}\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1}+\mathbf{w}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{1}+c. (89)

Then, substituting Eq. (88) into Eq. (89), we finally obtain

E~−𝐪,𝐪(2)=−𝐰†​𝐀−1​𝐰+c+(−b𝐰†𝐀−1𝐮+(c.c.))1+a​𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮+−|b|2​𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮+a​|𝐰†​𝐀−1​𝐮|21+a​𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮.\tilde{E}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{(2)}=-\mathbf{w}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{w}+c+\frac{(-b\mathbf{w}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}+(c.c.))}{1+a\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}}\\ +\frac{-|b|^{2}\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}+a|\mathbf{w}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}|^{2}}{1+a\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}}. (90)

A.2 Macroscopic dielectric constant

From Eq. (B3) of Ref. 20 and Eq. (71), we can deduce that the second-derivative of the total energy with respect to a monochromatic electric field of wavevector located inside the first Brillouin zone is

E−𝐪,𝐪e​f​(2)=Ω0(2​π)3​∫B​Zd​𝐤​∑no​c​csn​(⟨un​𝐤,𝐪(1)|H𝐤+𝐪,𝐤+𝐪(0)−εn​𝐤(0)|un​𝐤,𝐪(1)⟩+⟨un​𝐤,𝐪(1)|un​𝐤(0)⟩+⟨un​𝐤(0)|un​𝐤,𝐪(1)⟩)+2​π​Ω0​|n𝐪(1)​(𝐆=0)|2𝐪2+12∫Ω0d2​(n​εx​c)d​n2|n(0)​(𝐫)|n𝐪(1)(𝐫)|2d𝐫+2πΩ0∑𝐆≠0|n𝐪(1)​(𝐆)|2|𝐪+𝐆|2=𝐱†𝐀𝐱+𝐱†𝐮+𝐮†𝐱+a(𝐮†𝐱)(𝐱†𝐮),E^{ef(2)}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}=\frac{\Omega_{0}}{(2\pi)^{3}}\int_{BZ}d\mathbf{k}\sum_{n}^{occ}s_{n}\Big(\langle u_{n\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}|H_{\mathbf{k+q,k+q}}^{(0)}-\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|u_{n\mathbf{k,q}}^{(1)}\rangle+\langle u_{n\mathbf{k,q}}^{(1)}|u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}\rangle+\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}|u_{n\mathbf{k,q}}^{(1)}\rangle\Big)+2\pi\Omega_{0}\frac{|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G}=0)|^{2}}{\mathbf{q}^{2}}\\ +\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega_{0}}\frac{d^{2}(n\varepsilon_{xc})}{dn^{2}}\bigg|_{n^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})}|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}d\mathbf{r}+2\pi\Omega_{0}\sum_{\mathbf{G}\neq 0}\frac{|n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{G})|^{2}}{|\mathbf{q+G}|^{2}}=\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x})(\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{u}), (91)

where we have used the short-hand notation defined before. In the same spirit as Eq. (77), we can find the value of 𝐱\mathbf{x} that minimizes Eq. (91) (that we will call 𝐱2\mathbf{x}_{2}) and deduce

𝐀𝐱2+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱2)​𝐮+𝐮=0,\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_{2}+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{2})\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u}=0, (92)

which gives

𝐱2=(−a⁡(𝐮†​𝐱2)−1)​𝐀−1​𝐮.\mathbf{x}_{2}=(-a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}_{2})-1)\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}. (93)

Multiplying Eq. (92) by 𝐮†\mathbf{u}^{\dagger} and isolating 𝐱2\mathbf{x}_{2} allows us to obtain

𝐱2=−𝐀−1​𝐮1+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮).\mathbf{x}_{2}=-\frac{\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}}{1+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u})}. (94)

Substituting Eq. (92) and then Eq. (94) into Eq. (91), we obtain the value of E−𝐪,𝐪e​f​(2)E^{ef(2)}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}} at the minimum 𝐱2\mathbf{x}_{2}

E~−𝐪,𝐪e​f​(2)=𝐮†​𝐱2=−𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮1+a⁡(𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮).\tilde{E}^{ef(2)}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}_{2}=-\frac{\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}}{1+a(\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u})}. (95)

We can also define a total energy where the divergent 𝐆=0\mathbf{G}=0 Hartree contribution has been removed. The resulting term is analytic

E−𝐪,𝐪e​f,a​n​(2)\displaystyle E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{ef,an(2)} =𝐱†​𝐀𝐱+𝐱†​𝐮+𝐮†​𝐱,\displaystyle=\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}, (96)
=𝐮†​𝐱+𝐱†​(𝐀𝐱+𝐮).\displaystyle=\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\!\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\!(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{u}). (97)

The location 𝐱3\mathbf{x}_{3} of the minimum of E−𝐪,𝐪e​f,a​n​(2)E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{ef,an(2)} can be obtained in a similar way to Eq. (94)

𝐀𝐱3+𝐮=0⇒𝐱3=𝐀−1​𝐮.\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}_{3}+\mathbf{u}=0\Rightarrow\mathbf{x}_{3}=\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}. (98)

Substituting Eq. (98) into Eq. (96), we obtain the value of E−𝐪,𝐪e​f,a​n​(2)E_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{ef,an(2)} at the minimum 𝐱3\mathbf{x}_{3}

E~−𝐪,𝐪e​f,a​n​(2)=−𝐮†​𝐀−1​𝐮.\tilde{E}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{ef,an(2)}=-\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}^{-1}\mathbf{u}. (99)

Comparing Eqs. (95) and (99), we deduce

E~−𝐪,𝐪e​f​(2)=E~−𝐪,𝐪e​f,a​n​(2)1−a​E~−𝐪,𝐪e​f,a​n​(2).\tilde{E}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{ef(2)}=\frac{\tilde{E}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{ef,an(2)}}{1-a\tilde{E}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}}^{ef,an(2)}}. (100)

The polarizability χ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)\chi(\mathbf{r,r^{\prime}}) is defined as the microscopic response to a change of external potential that gives the total change of electronic density δ​n​(𝐫)\delta n(\mathbf{r})

δ​n​(𝐫)\displaystyle\delta n(\mathbf{r}) =∫Ω0χ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)​δ​ve​x​t​(𝐫′),\displaystyle=\int_{\Omega_{0}}\chi(\mathbf{r,r^{\prime}})\delta v_{ext}(\mathbf{r^{\prime}}), (101)
⇒δ​n​(𝐫)δ​ve​x​t​(𝐫′)\displaystyle\Rightarrow\frac{\delta n(\mathbf{r})}{\delta v_{ext}(\mathbf{r^{\prime}})} =χ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′).\displaystyle=\chi(\mathbf{r,r^{\prime}}). (102)

Transforming to reciprocal space and taking the (𝐆,𝐆′)=(𝟎,𝟎)(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}^{\prime})=(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{0}) matrix element yields

n𝐪(1)​(𝐆=𝟎)=χ𝐪​(𝐆=𝟎,𝐆′=𝟎),n^{(1)}_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{0})=\chi_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{0},\mathbf{G}^{\prime}=\mathbf{0}), (103)

where the (1)(1) superscript refers to the first-order perturbation in the external potential due to the electric field. Taking a long wavelength monochromatic electric field as the perturbation

ve​x​t,𝐪(1)​(𝐫,𝐫′)=ei​𝐪⋅𝐫​δ​(𝐫,𝐫′),v^{(1)}_{ext,\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{r,r^{\prime}})=e^{i\mathbf{q\cdot r}}\delta(\mathbf{r,r^{\prime}}), (104)

which gives in reciprocal space

ve​x​t,𝐤+𝐪,𝐤(1)​(𝐆,𝐆′)=δ𝐆,𝐆′,v^{(1)}_{ext,\mathbf{k+q,k}}(\mathbf{G,G^{\prime}})=\delta_{\mathbf{G,G^{\prime}}}, (105)

Eq. (95) tells us that

E~−𝐪,𝐪e​f​(2)\displaystyle\tilde{E}^{ef(2)}_{\mathbf{-q},\mathbf{q}} =𝐮†​𝐱2,\displaystyle=\mathbf{u}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}_{2}, (106)
=Ω02​n𝐪(1)​(𝟎),\displaystyle=\frac{\Omega_{0}}{2}n_{\mathbf{q}}^{(1)}(\mathbf{0}), (107)
=Ω02​χ𝐪​(𝟎,𝟎),\displaystyle=\frac{\Omega_{0}}{2}\chi_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{0}), (108)

where the second and third equalities stem from Eqs. (71) and (103), respectively.

The dielectric function is defined as (see Eq. (23) of Ref. 71 for example)

ε𝐪−1​(𝐆,𝐆′)=δ𝐆,𝐆′+4​π|𝐪+𝐆|2​χ𝐪​(𝐆,𝐆′),\varepsilon_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1}(\mathbf{G,G^{\prime}})=\delta_{\mathbf{G,G^{\prime}}}+\frac{4\pi}{|\mathbf{q+G}|^{2}}\chi_{\mathbf{q}}(\mathbf{G,G^{\prime}}), (109)

and the macroscopic dielectric function, which is an average response to an applied field is (see Eq. (15) of Ref. 71 for example)

εM​(𝐪)=1ε𝐪−1​(𝟎,𝟎).\varepsilon_{M}(\mathbf{q})=\frac{1}{\varepsilon_{\mathbf{q}}^{-1}(\mathbf{0,0})}. (110)

Therefore, using Eqs. (72), (108), and (109), we obtain

Appendix B Behavior of the ZPR with the shifted parabola model

In this appendix, we study the behavior of the shifted parabola energy model presented in Eq. (35) to mimic the ZPR of polar and non-polar materials at points of the BZ that are not VBM nor CBM.

In spherical coordinates, Eq. (35) can be re-expressed as

ε⁡(𝐪)=q2−2​q​q0​cos⁡θ\varepsilon(\mathbf{q})=q^{2}-2qq_{0}\cos\theta (144)

where we have chosen the shift 𝐪0\mathbf{q}_{0} along the zz-Cartesian axis. This function vanishes when 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 or q=2​q0​cos⁡θq=2q_{0}\cos\theta. The last root is a sphere centered around 𝐪𝟎\mathbf{q_{0}} with radius q0q_{0}.

B.1 Integration on the spherical shell of poles

In this section, the ZPR of a polar material is analyzed in the case δ=0\delta=0. The set of poles of the ZPR is located on a sphere centered around 𝐪=𝐪𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{q_{0}}. We can introduce the new variable 𝐪~=𝐪−𝐪𝟎\mathbf{\tilde{q}}=\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{q_{0}} and express the ZPR as an integral on a sphere of radius qcq_{c}

∫0qcd​q~​∫0πd​θ​∫−ππd​ϕ​sin⁡(θ)(𝐪~+𝐪𝟎)2​q~2q~2−q02=2​π​∫0qcd​q~​q~2q~2−q02​∫0πd​θ​sin⁡θq~2+2​q​q0​cos⁡θ+q02.\int_{0}^{q_{c}}d\tilde{q}\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}d\phi\frac{\sin(\theta)}{(\mathbf{\tilde{q}}+\mathbf{q_{0}})^{2}}\frac{\tilde{q}^{2}}{\tilde{q}^{2}-q_{0}^{2}}\\ =2\pi\int_{0}^{q_{c}}d\tilde{q}\frac{\tilde{q}^{2}}{\tilde{q}^{2}-q_{0}^{2}}\int_{0}^{\pi}d\theta\frac{\sin\theta}{\tilde{q}^{2}+2qq_{0}\cos\theta+q_{0}^{2}}. (145)

The radial part of Eq. (145) can be integrated to

−2​πq0∫0qcdq~q~q~2−q02ln(|q~+q0||q~−q0|).-\frac{2\pi}{q_{0}}\int_{0}^{q_{c}}d\tilde{q}\frac{\tilde{q}}{\tilde{q}^{2}-q_{0}^{2}}\ln\Big(\frac{|\tilde{q}+q_{0}|}{|\tilde{q}-q_{0}|}\Big). (146)

As we would like to understand the behaviour of the poles when integrated, we restrict the integral on a small spherical shell around q~=0\tilde{q}=0 with q0−Δ<q~<q0+Δq_{0}-\Delta<\tilde{q}<q_{0}+\Delta. Expressing everything in terms of a new variable u=q~−q0u=\tilde{q}-q_{0}, we deduce

that may be rewritten as

∫−ΔΔd​u​F​(u)​1u+G⁡(u)​ln⁡(|u|)u,\int_{-\Delta}^{\Delta}duF(u)\frac{1}{u}+G(u)\frac{\ln(|u|)}{u}, (148)

with

2​π​∫0qcd​q​q4​q0​ln⁡((q2+2​q​q0+ω)2+δ2(q2−2​q​q0+ω)2+δ2).2\pi\int_{0}^{q_{c}}dq\frac{q}{4q_{0}}\ln\bigg(\frac{(q^{2}+2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}+\delta^{2}}{(q^{2}-2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}+\delta^{2}}\bigg). (157)

When δ=0\delta=0, this function behaves quadratically when qq tends to 0 because the lowest order of the Taylor expansion of the logarithm is linear in qq. Therefore, the integral on a sphere of radius Δ\Delta of this function is

∫0Δd​q​q4​q0​ln⁡((q2+2​q​q0+ω)2(q2−2​q​q0+ω)2)=C​Δ3+𝒪⁡(Δ4).\int_{0}^{\Delta}dq\frac{q}{4q_{0}}\ln\bigg(\frac{(q^{2}+2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}}{(q^{2}-2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}}\bigg)=C\Delta^{3}+\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{4}). (158)

However, for polar materials, the function to integrate is similar to a Lindhard function

14​q​q0​ln⁡((q2+2​q​q0+ω)2+δ2(q2−2​q​q0+ω)2+δ2).\frac{1}{4qq_{0}}\ln\bigg(\frac{(q^{2}+2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}+\delta^{2}}{(q^{2}-2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}+\delta^{2}}\bigg). (159)

This function actually tends to a finite value because of the linear behavior of the logarithm in qq that cancels the denominator. Eq. (159) for δ=0\delta=0 gives

∫0Δ14​q​q0​ln⁡((q2+2​q​q0+ω)2(q2−2​q​q0+ω)2)=A​Δ+𝒪⁡(Δ2).\int_{0}^{\Delta}\frac{1}{4qq_{0}}\ln\bigg(\frac{(q^{2}+2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}}{(q^{2}-2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}}\bigg)=A\Delta+\mathcal{O}(\Delta^{2}). (160)

B.3 Integration on a spherical shell around q=0q=0

In this section, we focus only on the δ\delta-behavior of polar materials in the non-adiabatic framework, where Eq. (159) has to be integrated.

The integrand has 3 poles: when q=0q=0, and at the two real roots (if any) of q2−2​q​q0+ωq^{2}-2qq_{0}+\omega, which we call q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} with q1<q2q_{1}<q_{2}.

Actually, when q=0q=0, the integrand does not diverge when δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0, as shown in the subsection B.2. We will here focus on q=q2q=q_{2} as the behavior with respect to δ\delta in q=q1q=q_{1} is similar.

The integration around q2q_{2} is given by

2​π​∫q2−Δq2+Δd​q​14​q​q0​ln⁡((q2+2​q​q0+ω)2+δ2(q2−2​q​q0+ω)2+δ2).2\pi\int_{q_{2}-\Delta}^{q_{2}+\Delta}dq\frac{1}{4qq_{0}}\ln\bigg(\frac{(q^{2}+2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}+\delta^{2}}{(q^{2}-2qq_{0}+\omega)^{2}+\delta^{2}}\bigg). (161)

We introduce the change of variable u=q−q2u=q-q_{2}, and we consider δ≪Δ≪q2\delta\ll\Delta\ll q_{2}

2​π​∫−ΔΔd​u​14​q2​q0​ln⁡(((q1+q2)​(2​q2))2((q2−q1)​(u))2+δ2).2\pi\int_{-\Delta}^{\Delta}du\frac{1}{4q_{2}q_{0}}\ln\bigg(\frac{((q_{1}+q_{2})(2q_{2}))^{2}}{((q_{2}-q_{1})(u))^{2}+\delta^{2}}\bigg). (162)

This integral can be expressed as

2​π4​q2​q0​(2​Δ​ln⁡(4​(q1+q2)​q22)−2​Δ​ln⁡(δ2)CLOSE−∫−ΔΔduln(u2​(q2−q1)2δ2+1)),\frac{2\pi}{4q_{2}q_{0}}\bigg(2\Delta\ln\Big(4(q_{1}+q_{2})q_{2}^{2}\Big)-2\Delta\ln(\delta^{2})\\ -\int_{-\Delta}^{\Delta}du\ln\Big(\frac{u^{2}(q_{2}-q_{1})^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+1\Big)\bigg), (163)

and evaluated as

2​π4​q2​q0​(2​Δ​ln⁡(4​(q1+q2)​q22)−2​Δ​ln⁡(δ2)CLOSE−δq2−q1​2​Δ​(q2−q1)δ​(ln⁡(Δ2​(q2−q1)2δ2+1)−2)OPEN−δq2−q1​4​tan−1⁡(Δ⁡(q2−q1)δ)).\frac{2\pi}{4q_{2}q_{0}}\Bigg(2\Delta\ln\Big(4(q_{1}+q_{2})q_{2}^{2}\Big)-2\Delta\ln(\delta^{2})\\ -\frac{\delta}{q_{2}-q_{1}}\frac{2\Delta(q_{2}-q_{1})}{\delta}\bigg(\ln\Big(\frac{\Delta^{2}(q_{2}-q_{1})^{2}}{\delta^{2}}+1\Big)-2\bigg)\\ -\frac{\delta}{q_{2}-q_{1}}4\tan^{-1}\Big(\frac{\Delta(q_{2}-q_{1})}{\delta}\Big)\Bigg). (164)

As Δ/δ\Delta/\delta is large, Eq. (164) reduces to

2​π4​q2​q0​(2​Δ​ln⁡(4​(q1+q2)​q22)−2​Δ​ln⁡(δ2)CLOSE−δq2−q1​2​Δ​(q2−q1)δ​2​ln⁡(Δ⁡(q2−q1)δ)OPEN−δq2−q1​4​π2),\frac{2\pi}{4q_{2}q_{0}}\bigg(2\Delta\ln\big(4(q_{1}+q_{2})q_{2}^{2}\big)-2\Delta\ln(\delta^{2})\\ -\frac{\delta}{q_{2}-q_{1}}\frac{2\Delta(q_{2}-q_{1})}{\delta}2\ln\Big(\frac{\Delta(q_{2}-q_{1})}{\delta}\Big)\\ -\frac{\delta}{q_{2}-q_{1}}4\frac{\pi}{2}\bigg), (165)

which behaves as

C1−C2​δ.C_{1}-C_{2}\delta. (166)

The same reasoning applies when ω=0\omega=0. In this case the poles are q1=0q_{1}=0 and q2=2​q0q_{2}=2q_{0}. The ZPR behavior of a non-extremum point in the Brillouin Zone is thus linear in the non-adiabatic and in the static case with respect to δ\delta.
